clue.text: Bless errant ancestor entering church …

indicators.note: entering says the rearranged word goes inside the church abbreviation

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: errant means wandering astray, so the letters of ancestor stray into a new order

explanation.surface: A wayward forebear wanders into church and is blessed, the trailing dots carrying the scene on to the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'errant' signals the anagram and 'entering' the container; CE, the Church of England, is the usual crossword church.
explanation.definitionFit: To consecrate is to make holy by a religious rite, a synonym of bless in its sacred sense.

clue.text: 'Carry On Constable' goes over expert's head

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece that goes over another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: cop is slang for a police officer such as a constable

indicators.note: head means the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Echoes the film Carry On Constable, as if a policeman outranks an expert.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotes dress up 'Carry On Constable', a British comedy film, but 'Carry On' is the definition and 'Constable' gives COP.
explanation.definitionFit: To cope is to manage and keep going despite difficulty, which is to carry on.

clue.text: Vernon's to perform in part without a break

indicators.note: in part says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Vernon is due to play a piece without an interval.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts in 'Vernon's' and ends in 'perform'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done non-stop continues without pause, ceasing at no point along the way.

clue.text: Musical style is gentle, say, in broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters of the words are strewn into a new order

explanation.surface: A kind of music is described as soft when it goes out on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' rearranges IS GENTLE SAY IN; 'say' looks like it marks an example but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy listening is a genre of soft, melodic popular music, so it is a style of music.

clue.text: Stood down, and joined again

definitions.meaning: to stand down is to quit a post
... means signed up again for the same club or contract

explanation.surface: Someone left the job and then came back to it.
explanation.definitionFit: One spelling, two senses: having quit a post, and re-signed, put a name to a contract a second time.

clue.text: Article cheers Greek character

parts.note: the is the definite article
ta and cheers are both British informal thanks

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece applauds a person from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character' means a letter of the alphabet, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet, so it is a written character.

clue.text: … part of which is despairing somewhat when backsliding

indicators.note: backsliding means going backwards, so the run of letters is read right to left
somewhat says only some of the next word's letters are used, a run inside it

explanation.surface: Continuing the church scene: part of the congregation is in despair and lapsing from the faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somewhat' takes ESPA from inside 'despairing', and 'when backsliding' turns it round. 'which' points back to the church of 1 across through the dots.
explanation.definitionFit: The apse is the vaulted semicircular end of a church, so it is one part of the building consecrated in 1 across.

clue.text: Suggest writing about work

indicators.note: about means around, so the writing surrounds the work

parts.note: prose is ordinary written language
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Pitch an idea for a piece written about a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'on the subject of' but is the container signal; 'work' is the usual crossword opus.
explanation.definitionFit: To propose is to put forward an idea for consideration, a synonym of suggest.

clue.text: Fundamental part of detective's catchphrase?

definitions.meaning: basic or rudimentary, as in first principles
Sherlock Holmes is credited with the line beginning with this word, followed by my dear Watson

explanation.surface: A question about the key part of a famous sleuth's line.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: basic or rudimentary, and the opening word of Sherlock Holmes's famous phrase to Watson.

clue.text: Criticise guests on vacation — they're painful

parts.note: to pan a show is to criticise it harshly

indicators.note: on vacation means emptied out, so only the outer letters of the word stay

explanation.surface: A host complains about the guests who have left, finding them a pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on vacation' means emptied of contents: only the outer letters of 'guests' survive.
explanation.definitionFit: Pangs are sudden sharp spasms of pain or emotion, so they are the things that hurt.

clue.text: Deserve to bust docker

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the letters of the two words are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: A hint that a dock worker has earned a police raid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' rearranges DESERVETO, 'to' included, to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A stevedore loads and unloads ships, the same job as a docker or longshoreman.

clue.text: Former teetotaller, not professional, is show-off

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-husband

indicators.note: not says the professional is taken out of the teetotaller word

parts.note: a prohibitionist campaigns to ban alcohol, so is a teetotaller
pro is short for professional

explanation.surface: A one-time abstainer, now an amateur, likes to be the centre of attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes PRO from PROHIBITIONIST to leave HIBITIONIST.
explanation.definitionFit: An exhibitionist behaves so as to attract attention, the very definition of a show-off.

clue.text: Support for Cable from newspaper, European

parts.note: the Telegraph is a British daily newspaper, the one printing this puzzle
a Pole is a person from Poland, a European

explanation.surface: Reads as a newspaper's backing for a politician named Cable, with a European angle.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital C makes 'Cable' look like Vince Cable, a British Liberal Democrat politician, but it is a wire strung between posts.
explanation.definitionFit: A telegraph pole is the tall wooden post that holds up overhead telephone wires.

clue.text: Kitchen gadget — 51 nicker is ultimately expensive gear

parts.note: LI is 51 in Roman numerals
nicker and quid are both British slang for a pound sterling

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the last letter of each of the two words is taken

explanation.surface: A kitchen appliance costing 51 pounds is pricey kit after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nicker' is British slang for a pound, which is also a quid. 'ultimately' takes E and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A liquidiser is the British name for a blender, an appliance found in a kitchen.

clue.text: Firm regularly gets past deadlocks

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of the word before it, here the second and fourth

parts.note: to pass is to get past, as one car passes another

explanation.surface: A company keeps overcoming standoffs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes IM from the even letters of 'Firm'.
explanation.definitionFit: An impasse is a situation where no progress is possible, a stalemate between parties.

clue.text: Lacking muscles, went topless

parts.note: abs is short for abdominal muscles

indicators.note: topless means without its top, so the first letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: went is the past of go

explanation.surface: Someone without a six-pack went shirtless anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' drops the W of 'went' to leave ENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Absent means missing or not present, so a quality that is absent is lacking.

clue.text: Cook too little grub initially for such as David

parts.note: to underdo meat is to cook it too little

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the first letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Instructions for barely cooking some food.
explanation.walkthrough: David is the biblical shepherd boy who beat the giant Goliath against the odds.
explanation.definitionFit: An underdog is the contestant expected to lose, exactly as David was against Goliath.

clue.text: 60% of routine is odd

indicators.note: sixty per cent of a ten-letter word keeps its first six letters and loses the last four

parts.note: routine in the sense of ordinary and humdrum is uneventful

explanation.surface: A statement that part of a routine is strange.
explanation.walkthrough: The synonym is UNEVENTFUL; '60% of' keeps its first six letters, dropping TFUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Uneven numbers are odd ones, and uneven can also mean irregular or strange.

clue.text: Observe energy's needed to lead the old dance

indicators.note: needed to lead says the energy letter goes at the front of what follows

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
ye is an old spelling of the
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Someone is told vigour is needed to head a traditional dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the old' gives YE, the archaic form of 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball someone is to look at them hard, an informal synonym of observe.

clue.text: Ink and water ruined jumper, perhaps

indicators.note: ruined means spoilt and broken up, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Spilled ink and water have spoilt a sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges INK and WATER together. A jumper is the British word for a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: A jumper is one example of knitted clothing, hence the 'perhaps' marking an example.

clue.text: Obscure cuttings found in empty envelope

indicators.note: found in says the cuttings sit inside the emptied word
empty means hollowed out, so only the outer letters of the word stay

parts.note: clips are cuttings, as from a newspaper

explanation.surface: Odd press cuttings turn up inside an envelope with nothing else in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'empty' leaves only the outer letters of 'envelope', and 'found in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To eclipse is to block out or overshadow, a verb sense of obscure.

clue.text: Wheel tiny dodo out — it's incurable

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters of the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Bring out a tiny extinct bird on wheels, and hopeless with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges the letters of WHEEL TINY DODO.
explanation.definitionFit: Dyed-in-the-wool describes someone fixed in their ways, an inveterate case beyond reform, like an incurable romantic.

clue.text: Keep side-splitting introductions for Stan and Ollie in trunk

indicators.note: side-splitting is read as splitting off the sides, so the outer letters are lost

parts.note: to keep something is to store it

indicators.note: introductions are the opening letters of the two names

explanation.surface: Laurel and Hardy's hilarious openings stay in a box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'side-splitting' looks like 'hilarious' but means its sides are split off the synonym for keep. Stan and Ollie are Laurel and Hardy, the comedy pair.
explanation.definitionFit: The torso is the trunk of the human body, without head or limbs.

clue.text: Positive place, America

parts.note: PL is the abbreviation for place in street names
US is the United States

explanation.surface: A cheerful note about an American location.
explanation.definitionFit: A plus is a positive feature or advantage, and the plus sign marks a positive number.

clue.text: At intervals, walked unsteadily

definitions.meaning: ... hours or starts are arranged at spaced times rather than together
to stagger is to totter or lurch while walking

explanation.surface: Someone tottered along, pausing now and then.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: spread out in time, and tottered along like a drunk.

clue.text: Force terrible lie about politician

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged letters surround the politician
terrible means awful, so the letters of lie are mangled into a new order

parts.note: MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A dreadful lie about an MP is forced on the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' signals the anagram and 'about' the container, the shuffled letters wrapping the politician: IEL around MP.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel is to drive or urge someone on, a synonym of force as a verb.

clue.text: French cheese, but not posh part

indicators.note: but not says what follows is taken away from the cheese

parts.note: Roulé is a soft French cheese rolled with herbs
U means upper-class, so posh, in British usage

explanation.surface: A French cheese that is not a fancy one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but not' takes U out of ROULE.
explanation.definitionFit: A role is an actor's part in a play or film.

clue.text: Child has good accent, one warbles

parts.note: a son is a male child
an accent on a syllable is the stress placed on it

explanation.surface: A well-spoken child grows up to sing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' is only the link joining the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A songstress is a female singer, and to warble is to sing with trills.
